topic: The Physics of Pi: Block Collisions and Transcendental Digits

sections.title: The Hook: Surprising Collisions
sections.content: Introduce the setup: Two blocks on a frictionless surface. Block A has mass M, Block B has mass 1, and a wall sits to the left. We count the total number of collisions (A hitting B, B hitting the wall, B hitting A).
sections.example: If Block A is 100 times heavier than Block B, they collide exactly 31 times. If M = 10,000, they collide 314 times. If M = 1,000,000, they collide 3,141 times.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly explain the underlying physics: Conservation of momentum and kinetic energy. In 1D elastic collisions, this system maps to a motion in a 2D phase space. Visualize this as a ball bouncing inside a 'wedge' shape on a coordinate plane.
sections.example: Visualizing the phase space: The angle of the wedge is defined by the mass ratio; as the ratio grows, the wedge narrows, forcing the 'ball' to bounce more times before exiting.

sections.title: Connecting Physics to Geometry
sections.content: Explain that as the mass ratio M approaches infinity, the path length in the phase space approach a circular arc. The number of collisions corresponds to the digits of pi because the arc length relates to the angle calculation of the reflections.
sections.example: An animation showing a light ray bouncing between two mirrors angled at alpha = arctan(1/sqrt(M)). As M increases, the 'zig-zag' path traces the circumference of a circle.

sections.title: The Grand Reveal
sections.content: Synthesize the findings: The collision count is a digital manifestation of pi. This turns a discrete mechanical system into a tool for calculating transcendental numbers.
sections.example: Final slide showing a table: Mass M=10^2n -> Collisions = n digits of pi. It’s not magic; it’s the geometry of phase space!
